assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reaching the 10^-18 level turned laser-cooled atoms and the magic-wavelength idea into the most precise measurement devices ever built. This is atomic physics in its purest form, with direct consequences for redefining the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. It speaks to the measurement-limited view of progress: what can be measured, and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first Sr lattice clock; Jun Ye's group drove the systematic accuracy and coherence to the 10^-18 regime. Two laureates give a clean, defensible configuration. Other contributors (e.g. the Hall/Hansch comb lineage, ion-clock groups) are partly recognised already, and I cannot verify independently how much credit others in the supplied list would claim.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups worldwide, with international comparisons and redefinition-of-the-second roadmaps. Interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the redefinition of the second will be completed before the committee wants to act is not something I can verify.
The 2005 prize already recognised frequency combs, so the committee must judge whether clocks are sufficiently distinct.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type many-body models in controllable form, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition as the landmark. The field created a new experimental platform for condensed-matter and quantum-information questions, with single-site imaging as a further step.
assessment.attribution: The credited list has five names, so a selection is required. Zoller (with Jaksch and collaborators) supplied the key proposal, Greiner and Bloch the decisive experiments and the quantum gas microscope era. Esslinger and Cirac are strong but I leave them out to keep a compact trio; this exclusion is a real judgement call and would be contested.
assessment.maturity: Roughly two decades of replication and extension across many labs. The central results are robust, though some promised payoffs for open problems (e.g. high-Tc physics) remain unrealised.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among five prominent names is genuinely contested and partly overlaps with the Cirac-Zoller candidate.
The BEC prizes of 2001 and 1997 cooling prize reduce novelty somewhat.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry demonstrated matter-wave coherence with massive objects and became a sensor for gravity, rotation and tests of the equivalence principle and fundamental constants. It combines laser cooling, coherent beam splitting and precision measurement, squarely in the tradition of atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, Pritchard's early atom-optics demonstrations and Kasevich-Chu's light-pulse interferometer are all pivotal. The trio is natural, but priority between the 1991 demonstrations by several groups (including Mlynek and Helmcke) is not captured by the supplied credit and I am not sure of exact details.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with commercial and precision-gravimetry applications and large-scale fundamental-physics experiments. Some foundational claims, such as detecting gravitational waves or dark matter, are still prospective.
uncertainties: Other early 1991 groups are absent from the credited names, which could make the fair attribution contested.
Distinction from the 1989 Ramsey and 1997/2001 atomic prizes needs care.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled interfaces between light and matter (cavity QED with single atoms, atomic-ensemble memories, entanglement distribution) underpin quantum networks and repeaters. The concept of storing and retrieving quantum states of light is foundational for scalable quantum communication.
assessment.attribution: Kimble's quantum-network vision and DLCZ-related work, Rempe's single-atom cavity-QED node and photon-pistol experiments, and Lukin's EIT-based storage and ensemble work are all central. The compound nature, with several platforms (atoms, ions, solid-state), makes a fair selection of three delicate. Important contributors from other platforms, such as rare-earth-doped crystals, are not credited here. I work in this broader area and so should be cautious about my own judgement of priority.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are well confirmed in individual nodes and short-distance links, but practical long-distance networks are still developing; recognition may be somewhat early for the network-level claim yet is mature for the cavity QED foundations.
uncertainties: Compound discovery whose parts may merit different recognition.
Scope relative to related candidates that credit Lukin or Kimble for other topics, and my own field proximity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and precision spectroscopy of antihydrogen and antiprotons enable direct CPT and gravity tests. The techniques are demanding and the results (1S-2S, hyperfine, charge-to-mass comparisons) are of fundamental significance.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led antiproton trapping, cold antihydrogen (ATRAP) and precision work on the electron and positron magnetic moments; Hangst led ALPHA and its spectroscopy. Other collaborations (ATHENA, AEgIS, BASE and its leadership) are excluded by the supplied credit, so the allocation is not obviously exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Results are reproduced across collaborations at CERN's Antiproton Decelerator, and measurements keep improving. No violation of CPT is seen, so the impact is as precision confirmation and new capability.
uncertainties: Null results for new physics make the discovery framing less striking.
Missing credit for the BASE and ATHENA groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire laser and passive mode-locking made reliable femtosecond sources practical, enabling frequency combs, attosecond science and a large fraction of modern ultrafast spectroscopy. As an enabling invention its reach is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire gain medium, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking, and Keller developed SESAMs. These are distinct inventions, and the three-person configuration is defensible, though the Kerr-lens work involved other names not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and widely deployed. Recognition is late rather than premature, and the ultrafast and comb prizes have already drawn on this technology.
uncertainties: Several enabling inventions are bundled as one candidate.
Distinct priority claims for Kerr-lens mode-locking are not resolved in the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and readout of single nitrogen-vacancy spins in diamond created a room-temperature quantum sensor with nanoscale resolution for magnetic fields, temperature and biological samples. This links closely to the measurement-precision theme and shows real versatility.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's single-NV optical detection of magnetic resonance is the founding experiment; Lukin and Walsworth (with collaborators such as Yacoby and Hollenberg) delivered nanoscale magnetometry. Other leading names, notably Awschalom and Yacoby, are not credited, so the allocation looks incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and increasingly applied, though many of the headline biomedical and materials applications are still maturing, so recognition could be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Credit is distributed among more groups than the three supplied names.
Lukin appears on several candidates, so I should avoid overweighting a single person.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser exploits engineered intersubband transitions in semiconductor heterostructures to produce mid-infrared emission not tied to a bandgap. It enabled compact trace-gas spectroscopy, sensing and frequency-comb sources, a clear invention that changed laser spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs by Faist, Capasso, Cho and colleagues is well documented; Cho's molecular-beam epitaxy was essential for fabrication. The listed trio is plausible, though other Bell Labs co-authors (e.g. Sirtori, Sivco, Hutchinson) could be claimed and I cannot verify team contributions.
assessment.maturity: Mature, commercially established, with continuing performance gains (continuous-wave room-temperature operation, combs). Timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as invention-driven physics at the required level.
Credit among Bell Labs co-authors beyond the three supplied names.
